title: The Latest On CAR-T: Good and Bad
body_text: I’ve written many times about CAR-T cell therapies and some of the variations on this theme. Most recently I wrote back in the spring about some of the more allogenic idea being tried, i.e. ones that concentrate on using more off-the shelf approaches to preparing the modified T cells, as opposed to the usual procedure of taking the patient’s own cells, modifying them ex vivo. That has produced some dramatic successes, but it’s quite difficult and expensive. At the time, I mentioned that a company called Allogene was in trials with some ideas of this type, and since then the company has reported some encouraging results. Their trial to delay relapse in already-treated but susceptible lymphoma patients is ongoing, but an interim read at the enrollment of the 24th patient was encouraging enough for the FDA to give them a “Regenerative Medicine Advanced Therapy” designation to help speed up development. The company has also reported early trial results for allogenic CAR-T therapy against a solid tumor type, clear-cell renal carcinoma, and the results are overall encouraging. This was in a pretty heavily pre-treated population, but a single infusion showed an objective response rate of 31% in a situation where you might not have expected much of a response at all. The biggest tox worry, as it is with most of these T-cell ideas, was what’s called “immune effector cell–associated hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis-like syndrome” (IEC-HS). That’s a hyperinflammatory condition that is not really associated with the more widely-known cytokine-release syndrome. Tackling that is a problem for the whole field. There’s also been a lot of work on using CAR-T ideas for autoimmune disorders, as last blogged about here. Developments in this area have been very mixed indeed. A small company called Kyverna is looking to file for FDA approval for treatment of the rare “stiff person syndrome”, a neurological autoimmune condition driven by antibodies to a patient’s own glutamic acid decarboxylase enzymes. There are several other small companies working in this autoimmune area as well. But two big-pharma efforts have recently come to sudden halts due to toxicity problems, which has caused a lot of distress and confusion. Another possibility I mentioned in my earlier post was modifying T cells in situ through some sort of gene therapy approach. A report on this has just recently appeared, with a team in China treated several patients with neurological autoimmune disease with a lentivirus vector to get their T cells to recognize CD-19-expressing targets. The results were encouraging, with all the patient cohorts showing clinical and biochemical improvements at six months post-infusion. These patients also showed evidence of a full “B cell reset”, with good ol’ fashioned naive B cells replacing the self-targeting ones. This seems to have been a successful proof-of-concept study, and the obvious next step is to do this in larger patient populations, across different dosing regimens, with follow-up for longer periods of time. I would think that this sort of thing is already getting underway. . .
